title: Sequence-length occupancy probing: throughput harness and repeatability protocol
body:
Summary:

This note documents a targeted throughput benchmarking protocol that focuses on how input sequence-length distributions map to GPU occupancy and end-to-end throughput. The emphasis is on repeatability for cross-variant comparison (model versions, quantization, kernel changes) and on isolating occupancy-driven regressions that are frequently masked by naive warmup and batching strategies.

Why this matters:
- Throughput (tokens/sec) is not a single-number property — it depends heavily on sequence-length mixes, KV-cache hit patterns, and batching alignment.
- Many regressions we see in rollouts happen when the occupancy profile shifts (e.g., more mid-length requests cause inefficient kernel choices).
- We need a standard harness that reveals such changes reliably and is cheap to run in CI and nightly suites.

Goals for the protocol:
1) Produce stable, repeatable throughput numbers across runs (<= 2% run-to-run variance for steady-state scenarios).
2) Surface occupancy/latency anomalies tied to sequence-length changes and KV cache dynamics.
3) Be small and deterministic enough to run in pre-merge CI and scalable for nightly stress runs.

High-level approach:
- Use synthetic load generation with explicit sequence-length buckets and deterministic request seeds.
- Statistically separate warmup/priming phase from steady-state measurement; report both.
- Instrument GPU and runtime-level signals (SM occupancy, L2, memory bandwidth, per-layer latency breakdown) and correlate with token throughput.
- Maintain an immutable run manifest (seed, binary/hash, model id, machine config) that gets stored alongside results.

Test matrix (examples):
- uniform-short: 100% requests at 16 tokens (prompt+gen).
- uniform-long: 100% requests at 512 tokens.
- mixed-heavy-tail: 70% short (<=32), 20% med (96-192), 10% long (512).
- KV-cache-warm: repeated prefix patterns to simulate chat session cache hits.
- bursty-microburst: Poisson bursts with lambda tuned to achieve target concurrency spikes.

Load generator config (recommended fields):
- duration_s: 600  # wall-clock seconds per run
- ramp_up_s: 60    # soft ramp to target QPS to avoid coldstart noise
- steady_window_s: 420 # measurement window after ramp and warmup
- concurrency_target: integer or autoscale policy to fix target occupancy
- seq_length_distribution: explicit buckets with weights
- deterministic_seed: 64-bit hex string
- prompt_catalog_id: reference id for prompt corpus

Example JSON snippet used by loadgen (literal text to copy into harness):
{
  "duration_s": 600,
  "ramp_up_s": 60,
  "steady_window_s": 420,
  "concurrency_target": 48,
  "seq_length_distribution": [{"len": 16, "weight": 0.5}, {"len": 128, "weight": 0.3}, {"len": 512, "weight": 0.2}],
  "deterministic_seed": "0x5f2c7b9a",
  "prompt_catalog_id": "canned-v1"
}

Repeatability checklist (must do every run):
- Record git SHA for runtime, model artifact identifier, and container image digest.
- Fix and record deterministic_seed passed to loadgen; if using prompt catalog, snapshot the chosen prompts and store their hashes.
- Reboot or reset GPU counters between runs for long-nightly suites to avoid drift from prior noise.
- Use a fixed NUMA/CPU affinity and pin loadgen threads; log top-level cgroups and docker runtime args.
- Ensure no other tenant workloads are scheduled on the same host (dedicated test host).
- Run 3 independent runs for each scenario and compute median and interquartile ranges; if variance > 5% investigate.

Warmup and priming heuristics (sequence-aware):
- Two-stage priming: 1) model binary/JIT/kernels priming (cold binary warmup) — send a handful of long synthetic requests to trigger kernel compilation paths; 2) KV-cache priming (if measuring chat-style cache behavior) — replay a small set of prefixes until cache hit rate stabilizes.
- For sequence-mix scenarios, prime using the same distribution as the steady-state window rather than a single fixed length; this avoids artificial cache distributions.
- Avoid massive single-request priming that oversaturates caches and skews memory allocator behavior. Use paced priming (e.g., 1 request every 50ms) for the compilation stage.

Instrumentation and signals to collect:
- Runtime: per-token latency, scheduling queue depth, batch sizes over time, kernel selection logs (which kernel variant ran).
- GPU: SM occupancy %, average SM active warps, achieved occupancy histogram by kernel, memory bandwidth utilization, L2 cache hit rate, PCIe vs NVLink traffic.
- Host: CPU utilization per core, interrupt rates, network qdisc drops, NIC transmit/receive p95/p99 latencies, disk IO (if swap used).
- Application: KV cache hit ratio over time, batch composition (num requests per batch), serialization time (mutex contention), allocator fragmentation metrics.
- Traces: lightweight end-to-end traces aligned to token boundaries for a small sample (not all requests).

Profiling hooks and tools (recommended):
- CUPTI/NVIDIA Nsight Systems for kernel timelines and occupancy heatmaps.
- ncu (NVIDIA Compute Utility) for targeted kernel-level hotspotting.
- runtime-level event logs (turn on kernel selection debug at info level for one run).
- Llama/Transformer layer tracing: instrument matrix multiply and softmax times if possible.
- Simple calorimetry: measure energy/power if hardware supports it to correlate throttling with occupancy drops.

Interpreting common signatures:
- High SM occupancy + low throughput: memory-bound kernels (check sustained memory bandwidth).
- Low SM occupancy + low throughput: divergent work or small batch inefficiency -> increase batch or tune kernel tiling.
- High host CPU + low GPU utilization: serialization or batching logic on host is the bottleneck. Check request coalescing and batching timers.
- Throughput drop with longer sequences but no change in SM occupancy: look at increased memory footprint per attention KV cache leading to lower effective batch sizes.

Bottleneck isolation steps (rapid):
1) Re-run with single-sequence-length (fixed len) to remove distribution variance.
2) Pin batch size and run microbenchmarks for matmuls of shapes observed in production.
3) Capture kernel-selection logs to see whether a less-efficient kernel variant is chosen for the observed shape.
4) Turn off KV cache to measure pure compute throughput baseline.

Reporting format (CSV columns we keep in results DB):
- run_id, runtime_sha, model_id, machine_type, concurrency_target, seq_bucket, median_tokens_per_s, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, sm_occupancy_pct, mem_bw_gbps, kv_hit_rate, steady_window_s, seed

Failure modes we often hit and mitigations:
- Non-deterministic prompt sampling: always snapshot the prompt set hash and record prompt indices used during the run.
- Kernel jitter on first few invocations after long idle: extend binary priming and use JIT cache snapshots where supported.
- NIC buffer drops during microbursts: add headroom to NIC queue limits and throttle burst profiles in loadgen for CI.
- Noise from background scheduler tasks on bench hosts: move tests to dedicated pre-provisioned machines or use cpuset isolation.

Cost vs fidelity guidance:
- Quick CI: 180s runs, smaller concurrency (lower host cost), run a single scenario (mixed-heavy-tail) with strict deterministic seed.
- Nightly: 600s runs across 4 scenarios with 3 repeats each and full instrumentation.
- Full regression: multi-hour stress run with mixed region failover tests and A/B kernel comparisons.

Example run manifest (human-readable):
- run_id: seq-probe-2026-02-10-01
- runtime_sha: a1b2c3d4
- model_id: opt-6.7b-q4_0
- image_digest: sha256:...
- machine: g5.12xlarge-sim1
- loadgen_config: /artifacts/loadgen/seq-probe-01.json
- seed: 0x5f2c7b9a
- notes: "primed with same distribution for 120s; L2 counters reset before run"

Quick reproducibility script (pseudo-commands):
# assume bench host has gcloud/ssh access and bench container image created
ssh bench-host-01 "docker pull ghcr.io/redwood-inference/bench:latest && docker run --rm -v /tmp/artifacts:/artifacts ghcr.io/redwood-inference/bench:latest --manifest /artifacts/seq-probe/manifest.json"

Appendix: small troubleshooting checklist for SRE/bench runner:
- Are drivers and CUDA toolkit versions pinned? (yes/no)
- Has NVSHMEM/NVML been configured to collect metrics?
- Is the loadgen pinned to the same NUMA domain as the runtime process?
- Were previous runs terminated cleanly (no zombie processes holding GPU memory)?
- Does the run manifest include the exact kernel selection debug level?

A note on evolving the protocol:
We expect to iterate on distributions and add a standardized microtrace payload that captures the first 256 tokens of a sample of runs to allow offline per-token regression analysis. When changing load distributions, increment the manifest version and keep older manifests for historical comparison.

Action items:
- Ethan: implement deterministic prompt snapshot in loadgen (ENG-9821).
- Samir: add kernel-selection logging toggle to runtime and expose a lightweight parser for results.
- Mariana: add this protocol to nightly benchmark orchestrator and create result dashboards for the seq-length buckets.

End of document.
